# Introduction to Advanced Navigation {#intro}

Same math, from submarines to drones.

[Chapter: Introduction to Advanced Navigation](https://jbrodovsky.github.io/advanced_navigation/chapters/00-intro/intro.html)

## It was all the same math

[What do a submarine and a drone have in common?]{.question}

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- Penn State's Applied Research Laboratory: navigation for submarines
- Then a company building autonomous flying vehicles
- Modern robotics borrowed its navigation from aerospace and maritime engineering
:::

. . .

What changes is the **scale** of the problem and the **curvature of the Earth**.

::: {.notes}
The surprise from the first months at ARL: the big navigation systems of
submarines run on the same math as small robots. Machine versus robot is a
lecture on philosophy; skip it. This is a course on how a computer system works
out where it is by perceiving its environment, whether the answer goes to a
human navigator or to a robot's controller. (Intro chapter, "Why Write This
Course?")
:::

## About me

::: {.incremental}
- PhD candidate in mechanical engineering, Temple University: navigation without

- Before that: Penn State ARL, for the Office of Naval Research and the
  submarine fleet
- Philadelphia, US Eastern time (same as Worcester)
- I aim to reply within 24 h on weekdays, 48 h on weekends
- Minor debugging help: on the discussion boards, not one-on-one
:::

::: {.notes}
Online students are spread over many time zones, so be patient with replies.
Urgent: email or the Canvas discussion boards. Debugging support is in Python

Inspired by Roger Labbe's *Kalman and Bayesian Filters in Python*: every idea
gets a Python implementation you can run.

. . .

| Executed Python block | runnable example | it runs; any randomness is seeded |
| Marked `eval: false` | interface sketch | the shape, not the full implementation |

A concise contract beats a deceptively incomplete "complete system."

Executed blocks run every time the book renders. Python because it makes

# Guidance, Navigation, and Control {#gnc}

The boundaries are where real systems break.

[Chapter: Guidance, Navigation, and Control](https://jbrodovsky.github.io/advanced_navigation/chapters/00-intro/navigation-overview.html)

## Two vocabularies, one problem

[What does navigation owe the rest of the robot?]{.question}

. . .

| Aerospace and maritime | Robotics |
|---|---|
| Guidance | Path planning |
| Navigation | Localization |
| Control | Control |

. . .

Control is always control. If I ever call it something else, please inform my
wife: I have probably had a stroke.

::: {.notes}
Two fields invented and reinvented the same topics. Autonomous GNC sits between
manned aerospace and maritime engineering (semi-autonomous systems) and unmanned
robotics; the differences are the vocabulary, the applications, and whether a
human is in the decision loop. I will mix the terms; so does the literature.
:::

## Measurements, not facts

::: {.incremental}
- **Sensors:** IMU specific force and angular rate, GNSS, wheel counts, each
  stamped with the time it was **valid**, not the time the packet arrived
- **Perception:** feature tracks, landmark detections, PnP poses, scan matches
- **Maps and calibration:** intrinsics, lever arms, clock offsets
:::

. . .

Every measurement needs a noise model $\mathbf{R}$.
[A PnP pose without a covariance is a rumor.]{.accent}

. . .

::: {.key}
Get the calibration wrong and the estimator will helpfully "fix" it for you by
bending the trajectory.
:::

::: {.notes}
Project 1 Part B is an extended exercise in turning a perception algorithm into
a measurement with an honest R.
:::

## The output is a contract

::: {.smaller-text}
| Clause | What it contains | Who leans on it |
|----------|-------------------------------------|-----------------------|
| State | position, velocity, attitude, angular rate | everyone downstream |
| Frames | a named frame for every quantity (which NED origin?) | anyone who transforms states |
| Covariance | uncertainty consistent with the actual errors | planners, gating, mission logic |
| Time | when the state is valid; its latency when published | control, fusion |
| Rate | output rate and its jitter | control loops |
| Health | mode, active aids, NIS alarms, time since last fix | mission logic, operators |
:::

. . .

::: {.key}
A stale, unlabeled, or overconfident state is not a complete navigation solution.
:::

::: {.notes}
Every one of these clauses has caused a real failure somewhere when it was
missing.
:::

## The contract, as code

```{.python code-line-numbers="|3-4|5|6-9|10|11-14|1-14"}
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class NavSolution:
    t_valid: float          # time at which the state is valid [s]
    t_published: float      # time the message left the estimator [s]
    frame_id: str           # which NED frame p_n and v_n are expressed in
    p_n: np.ndarray         # position in n [m]
    v_n: np.ndarray         # velocity relative to Earth, resolved in n [m/s]
    q_bn: np.ndarray        # attitude q_b^n = [qw, qx, qy, qz]
    omega_b: np.ndarray     # bias-corrected angular rate in b [rad/s]
    P: np.ndarray           # error covariance, order [dp, dv, dtheta], (9, 9)
    mode: str               # e.g. "INS+GNSS", "INS coasting", "aligning"
    aids: tuple[str, ...]   # aiding sources used since the last message
    time_since_fix: float   # [s] since the last absolute position update
    nis_alarm: bool         # True if recent innovations fail the NIS test
```

Latency is `t_published - t_valid`. The point is not the syntax but the fields.

::: {.notes}
Walk through it: time, frame, state, covariance, health. Book conventions: NED
navigation frame n, FRD body frame b, Hamilton scalar-first quaternion, errors
defined as true minus estimate. The book's version adds `latency` and
`horizontal_sigma` helpers.
:::

## Different customers, different needs

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Control**

Smooth, high rate, low latency. A position step becomes a force step; a stale
state is phase lag.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Guidance and planning**

Global consistency and an honest covariance. 3σ margins are only as safe as the
σ.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Mission logic and operators**

Health: nominal, coasting on inertial, or failed? And for how long?
:::
::::

. . .

So many systems publish **two** products: a smooth, slowly drifting stream for
control, and a globally consistent pose that may jump, for planning. ROS calls
them `odom` and `map` (REP 105).

## Why we may draw boxes {auto-animate=true}

::: {data-id="plant"}
$$
\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{B}\mathbf{u},
\qquad
\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{x},
\qquad
\mathbf{u} = -\mathbf{K}_c\hat{\mathbf{x}}
$$
:::

::: {data-id="observer"}
$$
\dot{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} = \mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{B}\mathbf{u}
+ \mathbf{L}(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{H}\hat{\mathbf{x}}),
\qquad
\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{x} - \hat{\mathbf{x}}
$$
:::

A linear plant, an observer with gain $\mathbf{L}$, and a controller that acts
on the **estimate**, not the state.

## Why we may draw boxes {auto-animate=true}

::: {data-id="plant"}
$$
\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{B}\mathbf{u},
\qquad
\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{x},
\qquad
\mathbf{u} = -\mathbf{K}_c\hat{\mathbf{x}}
$$
:::

::: {data-id="separation"}
$$
\frac{d}{dt}
\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{x} \\ \mathbf{e} \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}\mathbf{K}_c & \mathbf{B}\mathbf{K}_c \\
\mathbf{0} & \mathbf{A} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{H}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{x} \\ \mathbf{e} \end{bmatrix}
$$
:::

. . .

Block triangular: the closed-loop eigenvalues are those of
$\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}\mathbf{K}_c$ together with those of
$\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{L}\mathbf{H}$.

. . .

::: {.key}
The estimation engineer and the control engineer can work in different buildings.
:::

::: {.notes}
For linear Gaussian systems with quadratic cost, the separation principle goes
further: the optimal controller is LQR applied to the Kalman filter's estimate
as if it were the truth (certainty equivalence). Exercise 5 derives the block
matrix.
:::

## Where the separation leaks

::: {.incremental}
- **Latency:** the estimate is valid at $t - \tau$ and arrives later still, a
  delay $e^{-s\tau}$ that neither designer accounted for
- **Nonlinearity:** separation holds only approximately, and observability
  depends on the trajectory (INS/GNSS heading while driving straight)
- **Overconfident covariances:** good measurements rejected at the gate, margins
  too thin, and a report that everything is fine
:::

. . .

Even when every assumption holds, separation promises optimality, not robustness.
Doyle (1978) on guaranteed stability margins for LQG regulators, in full:
[*"There are none."*]{.accent}

::: {.notes}
Doyle's note has a three-word abstract. Late measurements also produce
corrections that land as jumps, which is the next experiment.
:::

## One controller, four navigation feeds


A unit mass tracks a smooth reference: PD plus feedforward, $\omega_n = 4$ rad/s,
$\zeta = 0.7$, in a gusty wind. It sees only what navigation hands it:

::: {.incremental}
1. **truth**
2. **noisy:** unbiased white noise, 8 cm and 4 cm/s
3. **delayed:** perfect, but 150 ms old
4. **jumpy:** dead reckoning with a 5 cm/s velocity error, snapped back by a fix
   every 2 s
:::

. . .

All three imperfect feeds have an RMSE of roughly 6 to 8 cm.
[Which one flies worst?]{.accent}

::: {.notes}
Take a vote before moving on. The controller was designed assuming a perfect
state. The jumpy feed is what a filter does with sparse or late updates and no
smoothing of its corrections.
:::

150 ms of delay eats about 53° of a 65° phase margin; each fix is a step in the

::: {.key}
Bounded, reported latency; smoothed corrections; a usable output rate. These go

:::

## Four ways to know where you are

Robotics did not invent navigation.

::: {.smaller-text}
| Classical method | What it measures | Modern counterpart | In this course |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dead reckoning | heading, speed, elapsed time | wheel odometry, IMU mechanization, visual odometry | motion models; Project 1 Part A |
| Piloting | bearings and ranges to charted landmarks | landmark and map-based localization: AprilTags, tree trunks, lidar features | PnP, SLAM; Project 2 |
| Celestial | angles to bodies whose positions are predictable | star trackers, sun sensors | global navigation (ephemerides play the almanac) |
| Radio | timing or direction of radio signals | GNSS, ultra-wideband ranging | INS/GNSS; Project 3 |
:::

. . .

[SLAM is piloting with a chart you draw as you go.]{.accent}

::: {.notes}
Directions to a friend's house ("north two blocks, left at the gas station")
mix dead reckoning and piloting in one sentence. The standard reference for the
classical methods is Bowditch's *American Practical Navigator*, first published
in 1802 and still maintained by the U.S. government.
:::

Noon at the harbor mouth, due east at 6 knots: at 2 pm, 12 nmi east. Nothing observed.

The other three methods exist to bound that growth with fixes.

::: {.notes}
Errors grow without bound. Heading errors push you sideways; a fouled log pushes
you along track; current and leeway are worse, because a log measures speed
through the water and the heading says where the bow points, not where the ship
goes. Every distance is a speed times a time, so a bad clock corrupts everything.
A navigator distinguishes the DR position (ordered course and speed) from the
estimated position (allowing for current, leeway, and steering error): nominal
propagation versus one that accounts for disturbances, which is Part 4 in
miniature. "Dead" from "deduced" is probably a later invention, but a good
mnemonic. The fix every 6 h is an illustration, not a number from the chapter.
:::

## How flat is flat enough?


:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Travel $s$ along the surface; it falls below the flat tangent plane by

$$
d \approx \frac{s^2}{2R}, \qquad R \approx 6371 \text{ km}
$$

::: {.incremental}
- "Down" tilts by $s/R$: one arcminute per nautical mile
- Horizontal distances barely notice: millimeters at 10 km
:::
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}

[A flat frame: fine for a warehouse or a field, wrong across an ocean.]{.accent}

::: {.notes}
The vertical is what a flat-Earth model gets wrong; horizontal error grows like
s^3/R^2, a few millimeters at 10 km and a few meters at 100 km. History: Greek
writers took a spherical Earth seriously early; Eratosthenes, around 240 BCE,
got 250,000 stadia from noon shadows at Syene and Alexandria (within roughly 2
to 16 percent of the modern 40,075 km, depending on the stadion). Newton (1687)
argued for an equatorial bulge, confirmed by French expeditions in the 1730s and
1740s; WGS84 is the modern descendant. Large-scale navigation uses a frame that
moves with the vehicle (Part 6).
:::

## Latitude is easy; longitude is a clock problem

Latitude: one good sight of Polaris, or of the Sun at noon.

. . .

Longitude has no natural zero: the sky passes over every meridian in turn.

$$
\frac{360^\circ}{24 \text{ h}} = 15^\circ \text{ per hour}
$$

. . .

Local noon, and a clock keeping reference time reads 13:00: you are
**15° west** of the reference meridian.

. . .

Gemma Frisius proposed carrying such a clock in 1530. No clock of the day could
keep time at sea for weeks.

::: {.notes}
Before a solution: latitude sailing, which means reach the destination's latitude
and run east or west until something appears, hoping it is not rocks. Galileo
proposed the eclipses of Jupiter's moons as a sky clock (1610); fine on land,
hopeless on a rolling deck. Cassini's tables (1668) moved France's west coast
east on the maps; Louis XIV reportedly complained his astronomers had cost him
more territory than his enemies. Time zones, about 15° wide, are a fossil of the
same arithmetic. Units: one second of time is 15 arcseconds of longitude.
:::

## A clock worth £20,000

::: {.incremental}
- **1707:** a British fleet, unsure of its position, runs onto the Isles of
  Scilly. Four warships and well over a thousand sailors lost.
- **1714:** the Longitude Act. £10,000 for 1°, £15,000 for 40′, £20,000 for 30′.
- **1761--62:** Harrison's H4, 81 days to Jamaica, loses 5.1 s after allowing
  for its known rate
:::

. . .

$5.1 \text{ s} \times 15''/\text{s} = 76.5'' \approx 1.3'$ of longitude: roughly
a nautical mile.

. . .

The rival answer: lunar distances. A sextant, an almanac, and an hour of
arithmetic. Chronometers needed money.

::: {.notes}
Harrison, a self-taught Yorkshire clockmaker, spent four decades from H1 (1735)
to H4 (1759, about 13 cm across). He never received the prize as such;
Parliament granted him £8,750 in 1773. Lunars: Mayer's tables (1755) and
Maskelyne's Nautical Almanac (first edition for 1767). Cook carried Kendall's
copy of H4 on his second voyage. Around 1910, radio time signals finished the
problem by distributing the time instead of carrying it.
:::

## An accelerometer does not measure acceleration

Three gyros and three accelerometers, integrated: an INS is dead reckoning with
the physics done properly.

. . .

It measures **specific force**: non-gravitational force per unit mass, its
acceleration relative to free fall.

. . .

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
On a desk: about 9.8 m/s² **upward**, going nowhere.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
In free fall: **zero**, accelerating at 1 g.
:::
::::

. . .

::: {.key}
To recover acceleration, add gravity back. That requires knowing which way is
down, so attitude errors leak straight into velocity and position.
:::

::: {.notes}
"Most of what makes inertial navigation hard is that fact plus sensor bias."
Background: steel hulls and electrical machinery spoiled magnetic compasses,
hence the gyrocompass (Anschütz around 1908, Sperry in 1911, with Einstein as an
expert in their patent dispute). Specific force is developed in the motion
models chapter (Part 3).
:::

## Apollo: the architecture of this course

::: {.incremental}
- **1953:** Draper's MIT Instrumentation Laboratory flies a B-29 from
  Massachusetts to Los Angeles on inertial navigation alone
- **1958:** USS *Nautilus* crosses under the Arctic ice and the North Pole on an
  inertial system
- **Apollo:** the Primary Guidance, Navigation, and Control System, PGNCS
  ("pings"), from Draper's lab
- Its inertial platform drifted, so astronauts sighted stars through a sextant to
  realign it
:::

. . .

::: {.key}
A high-rate inertial solution kept honest by occasional external fixes: the
architecture of this entire course.
:::

## Satellites: clocks, again

::: {.incremental}
- **1957:** Guier and Weiffenbach (Johns Hopkins APL) find Sputnik's orbit from
  the Doppler shift of its beacon. Turn it around: a known orbit tells you where
  **you** are.
- **Transit:** operational 1964, open to civilian ships in 1967
- **GPS:** one-way ranging timed by atomic clocks. First satellite 1978, fully
  operational 1995.
:::

. . .

Harrison solved longitude with a good clock; GPS solves position the same way.
One nanosecond of timing error is about 30 cm of range.

. . .

::: {.aside-box}
The signals arrive weaker than the background radio noise, from 20,000 km away,
so they are easy to jam or spoof. In 2015 the U.S. Naval Academy put celestial
navigation back in its curriculum.
:::

## KAL 007: mode is part of the contract

::: {.incremental}
- **1 September 1983:** Korean Air Lines Flight 007 strays hundreds of
  kilometers off course into Soviet airspace and is shot down. All 269 people
  aboard are killed.
- The ICAO investigation: the crew most likely left the autopilot in heading-hold
  instead of letting the INS steer, and did not notice for more than five hours
- Two weeks later, President Reagan announced GPS for civil use once complete
:::

. . .

::: {.key}
A navigation system is only as good as the rest of the stack's awareness of what
mode it is in. That is why mode and health are clauses of the contract.
:::

::: {.notes}
Second lesson: public infrastructure can grow out of a military program.
Selective Availability was switched off in May 2000, and GPS now shares the sky
with GLONASS, Galileo, and BeiDou. Exercise 3 asks what in your design would
make five hours in the wrong mode impossible to miss, and whose job it is to
notice.
:::

## The same pattern, with better hardware

**Propagate** with a motion model. **Correct** with fixes from outside. **Track**
how far to trust each.

. . .

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Harrison's customer:** a navigator who took a fix once a day and steered by
hand
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Ours:** a flight controller that wants a state and covariance fifty times a
second, and acts without asking
:::
::::

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- **Project 1:** inertial dead reckoning for a quadrotor, piloting off AprilTags
- **Project 2:** draw your own chart from the tree trunks of Victoria Park
- **Project 3:** an inertial navigator on a rotating, curved Earth, corrected by
  satellites
:::

::: {.notes}
Along the way IMUs prove noisy, biased, and temperamental. Much of the craft is
knowing exactly how wrong your sensors are and telling the rest of the stack the
truth about it.
:::

## By the end of the course

[What will you be able to do?]{.question}

::: {.incremental}
1. Place navigation in an autonomy stack: what it consumes, what it owes

4. Build landmark SLAM: data association, map growth, consistency
5. Integrate INS with GNSS on the curved Earth in an error-state filter
6. Evaluate accuracy, uncertainty, consistency, and cost, then report it
:::

a plot that looks good. Kalman-style means EKF, UKF, and error-state filters.
